writer:g0-pass-first:1.post:
Three agents, six tools each, and the same brand rule pasted into every prompt. That was the plan I threw out.

In G0 the six capabilities every agent needs now sit behind one MCP server with versioned contracts. A breaking contract change fails the contract tests until the version is bumped, so nobody changes a shape by accident.

The count that sold me: 16 integrations before the layer, 8 after. 24 copies of the shared rules down to 8.

And 157 tests run without network or a model call.

Where do your shared rules live today: in one place, or in every prompt?

#marketingops #aiagents #buildinpublic

writer:g1-hook-fix:1.post:

Four agents in sequence (Researcher, Summarizer, Editor, Writer) read 15 RSS feeds and pick items worth posting about. I built it twice: n8n first, then Python with the Claude Agent SDK.

What would you build first?

#marketingops #aiagents #n8n

fixes: The first line is a status update, not a reason to keep reading. Open with the duplication finding.

writer:g1-hook-fix:2.post:
7 rules were carried by more than one agent. I only found out because I built the same scout twice.

Four agents in sequence (Researcher, Summarizer, Editor, Writer) read 15 RSS feeds and produce a weekly digest. The n8n version carried every shared rule in every prompt; the duplication log made the cost visible.

The second build, in Python with the Claude Agent SDK, keeps one copy of each rule.

One detail I'd keep in any agent: items are marked seen only after the digest is written, so a failed run never silently drops anything.

Have you ever counted how many prompts carry the same rule?

#marketingops #aiagents #n8n

writer:g2-brand-fix:2.post:
My lead triage crew cannot send an email. Not "is told not to". Cannot.

An orchestrator decides which specialists to call for each new lead: an Enricher, a Qualifier and a Drafter. The follow-up email is left as a draft.

A PreToolUse hook denies anything shaped like a send, and the HubSpot interface has no send method. A prompt is a promise; an interface without the method is a guarantee.

Six bands decide what happens to a lead, one rule each, in one function. All leads are synthetic.

Where do you enforce your agent guardrails: in the prompt or in the system?

#marketingops #aiagents #hubspot

writer:g3-third-pass:3.post:
My agent gets 3 tries. On the fourth, a human gets the draft.

A Writer drafts a LinkedIn post, a Critic scores it against a rubric, and the loop repeats until the post passes or hits a cap of 3 passes.

Hitting the cap flags the draft for human review instead of shipping a best effort. That flag is the feature, not the failure.

And a malformed Critic response is caught by schema validation, not passed through as a pass.

What's your agent's stop condition?

writer:malformed-critic:1.post:
Items are marked seen only after the digest is written. That one ordering rule is why a failed run never loses anything.

My weekly scout runs four agents in sequence (Researcher, Summarizer, Editor, Writer) over 15 RSS feeds. A seen-items table makes sure a re-run never repeats an item.

Mark too early and a crash silently drops the week. Mark after the write and the worst case is a repeat you can see.

Where does your pipeline mark work as done?

#aiagents #marketingops #n8n

writer:topic-pass-cap:1.post:
A loop without a stop condition isn't an agent. It's a bill.

When a Writer and a Critic go back and forth, the question isn't whether the next draft is better. It's who decides when to stop, and what happens then.

A hard pass cap answers both. The agent gets a fixed number of tries, and when it runs out, a person gets the draft with a clear flag instead of a quiet best effort.

What's the stop condition on the agents you run?

#aiagents #marketingops
